core.title: Tests do not write to shared live state
core.given: Any test code (new or existing, any file name), where test context is the union of two independent criteria — any code the stack's test runner executes, and any code inside the stack's test-declaration constructs
core.when: The test mutates the shared process environment or writes to the filesystem, for any purpose
core.then: The test MUST NOT mutate the shared process environment nor write to a filesystem path that does not match the profile's allowed-write predicate (shared live state: anything a later test also sees).
prefer: Scope every write to a temp directory the test owns and cleans up.
Pass configuration explicitly instead of mutating the environment, e.g. construct the code under test with the test's settings handed in directly.
avoid: Mutating the shared process environment from a test — it looks local but is global, and is the most common, least obviously wrong form of pollution.
Writing to repository or other shared filesystem paths that later tests also see.
unless: The write targets a path that matches the profile's allowed-write predicate; the predicate alone decides the exception (whatever it matches is allowed, literal or computed), with no additional requirement that the path be test-owned or actually contained in a temp/fixture directory.
The operation is a read; only the write family is in scope.
core.why: A polluting test does not fail; it makes a DIFFERENT test fail later, often only under a different order, with the failure pointing at the victim rather than the culprit (displaced failure). That asymmetry is why this is the family's strict rule, matching core: finding one after the fact costs days.
evidence: The stack's discipline check reports no mutations of the shared process environment (the profile's environment-mutation idiom) in test code.
The check reports no write-family filesystem calls whose literal path does not match the profile's allowed-write predicate.
Suite passes regardless of test order (no displaced failures).
verification: A static discipline check (validator) scans all test code — existing and changed — where test context is any code the stack's test runner executes or any code inside the stack's test-declaration constructs, whatever the file name. It flags mutations of the shared process environment and write-family filesystem calls whose literal path does not match the profile's allowed-write predicate. The predicate is the sole exemption test: any literal path it matches is allowed, even without actual test ownership or containment; conversely, no ownership claim exempts a path the predicate does not match. The check's literal-path reach is a reporting limit of the static check, not the scope of the obligation.
Reads are never flagged; only the write family is in scope.

A computed (non-literal) path cannot be judged by the static check and is not reported — a detection limitation, not a permission: the normative prohibition in `then` covers every write outside the allowed-write predicate's scope, computed paths included; only the check cannot see them.
A diff-level change observer, when present, is only an optimization to surface new violations early; it does not restrict applicability — pre-existing tests are equally in scope.
Severity 4; disposition strict — the rule fails on every finding; there is no advisory mode and no ratchet baseline.

values: test (any code the stack's test runner executes, or any code inside the stack's test-declaration constructs, regardless of file name and change status — the profile's test context)
test file by name pattern (non-exhaustive pre-filter; patterns from the profile)
shared-live-state mutation in test code (existing or changed)
write-family filesystem call in test code

fires: Any test assigns to the shared process environment, for whatever purpose (configuration, feature flags, setup, or anything else).

Any test performs a write-family filesystem operation (write, append, directory creation, removal, etc.) with a literal path that does not match the profile's allowed-write predicate, for whatever purpose.
An existing (unchanged) test already contains such a mutation or write when the suite or file is checked.

Code in scope through either test-context criterion — executed by the test runner or inside the stack's test constructs — is in scope even when its file name matches none of the profile's pre-filter patterns; the patterns are a fast path, not the scope.
doesNotFire: A test only reads files or reads the environment.

A test writes to a literal path that matches the profile's allowed-write predicate (in this stack, any literal path containing an allowed marker — the marker match alone suffices; the path need not be test-owned nor actually inside a temp/fixture directory).
A test writes using a computed (non-literal) path — the static check cannot judge it and does not report it (a check limitation, not a permission; such a write can still violate the obligation).
Production (non-test) code sets environment variables or writes files.

The allowed-write predicate that operationally decides whether a write path is exempt: whatever the predicate matches is allowed, by that match alone, regardless of actual test ownership or containment; every other write target is shared live state. In this stack the predicate is a substring match on path markers (the static check can evaluate it only on literal paths).
Non-exhaustive name-pattern pre-filter for unit test files (a fast path only; the profile's test context governs scope).

neutralityNotes: Fixes applied across rounds. R3 (feedback): the literal-path restriction was removed from the NORMATIVE filesystem prohibition — core.then now forbids writing to any filesystem path that does not match the profile's allowed-write predicate, computed paths included, matching bun.json.then ('outside a temp directory', no literalness) and its doesNotFire[2] disclaimer that unreported non-literal paths are a detector limitation, not a permission; unless[0] is likewise path-based ('literal' dropped). The literal-path restriction survives only where it belongs: in the check's reporting — core:verification (stated there as a reporting limit of the static check, not the scope of the obligation) and core:evidence[1] — preserving the distinction between an unreported computed write (still a violation) and an allowed write (predicate-matched, genuinely exempt). The Bun profile's marker-based exceptions are retained via idiom.test_constructs#test_write_scopes (substring match on tmpdir, /tmp, import.meta.dir, __fixtures__, .tmp), with the marker match alone deciding exemption. R2 fixes retained: the allowed-write exception is defined operationally through the predicate (no ownership/containment condition — test ownership and cleanup are only prefer[0]); the test-language scope is profiled as tooling.language_scopes#test_files; the environment-mutation idiom lives at idiom.security#environment_mutation. Test context remains the union of runner-executed code (tooling.test_runner) and test-declaration-construct code (idiom.test_constructs#test_context). Still realization-specific: detector/finding ids, the concrete write-family fs call set (the neutral 'write-family filesystem call' is generic; the API surface is the detector's pattern), the concrete code samples, and the observer/test-block syntax. Severity and disposition stay in core verification per the notProfileKeys policy. The Bun path_glob fact stays re-typed to file_kind because the core activation fact vocabulary is closed.
